record.paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
record.original_question: Is there a fundamental lower bound on the computational cost of evaluating physically relevant path integrals with sign problems, and if such a bound exists, how is it related to the P versus NP question in computational complexity? In other words, is an exponentially hard sign problem an unavoidable feature of some theories rather than merely a symptom of inadequate algorithms?

evidence.quote: Is there a minimum computational cost for the path integral? If there is, how much? This question is related to the ‘P versus NP problem’, which is an unsolved problem in computer science regarding the computational complexity [1].
Although the P versus NP problem has not been solved yet, many people believe that P and NP are different and there is a problem that cannot be solved within a polynomial time.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider physically relevant path integrals (in the sense of Euclidean lattice formulations of quantum field theories or many-body quantum systems) of the form
   Z = ∑_C w(C),    ⟨O⟩ = (1/Z) ∑_C O(C) w(C),
where the weights w(C) are in general complex or non-positive, so that direct Monte Carlo sampling suffers from a "sign problem" (cancellations causing the signal-to-noise ratio to decay exponentially in the system volume and inverse temperature).

(a) Does there exist a fundamental, theory-dependent lower bound on the computational cost (as a function of system size, inverse temperature, and desired accuracy) for evaluating such path integrals when a sign problem is present? In particular, decide whether for some physically motivated families of theories an exponential growth of computational cost with system size is unavoidable for every possible algorithm (including all possible reformulations, contour deformations, dual variables, etc.), as opposed to merely reflecting limitations of currently known algorithms.

(b) Clarify the relationship between the existence of such a lower bound and the P versus NP problem: i.e., determine whether the impossibility of a generic polynomial-time algorithm for the sign problem can be established conditionally on P ≠ NP, or unconditionally, and identify the precise complexity class that captures the hardness of evaluating these path integrals.
artifact.status_search_result: Troyer and Wiese (Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201, 2005) proved that a generic solution to the fermionic sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo is NP-hard, so a polynomial-time generic algorithm would imply P = NP. This conditionally rules out a universal efficient solution. However, the broader question — whether for specific physically relevant theories (e.g. finite-density lattice QCD) an exponentially hard sign problem is provably unavoidable, and the unconditional resolution tied to the still-open P vs NP problem — remains open.

status_evidence.title: Computational complexity and fundamental limitations to fermionic quantum Monte Carlo simulations
status_evidence.snippet: The sign problem is shown to be NP-hard, implying that a generic solution would also solve all NP problems in polynomial time.
status_evidence.claim: Generic sign problem is NP-hard; conditional on P≠NP, no universal polynomial-time solution exists.

status_evidence.title: Numerical sign problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Troyer and Wiese showed that the sign problem is NP-hard in general, although case-by-case solutions are possible.
status_evidence.claim: Generic problem NP-hard; specific cases may be solvable; full unconditional resolution tied to P vs NP, which is open.
